definition: To settle a disagreement by having each side give up part of what it wants.
example: The buyer and seller agreed to compromise on a price between their two offers.
nuance: Both sides give ground when they compromise; when only one side yields, it concedes or capitulates. Don't mix it up with comprise, which means "to consist of."
prompt: Two roommates disagree about how warm to keep their shared apartment.
options: The roommates agreed to compromise, setting the thermostat halfway between their choices.
To compromise, Maya refused to move the thermostat even one degree.
They chose to compromise by giving the louder roommate exactly the temperature he wanted.
Three small bedrooms and a narrow kitchen compromise the entire apartment they share.
reasons: Each person gives up a few degrees, so both sides yield and meet in the middle.
Refusing to give any ground is the opposite of meeting someone partway.
When one side gets everything and the other gets nothing, that is giving in, not a middle ground.
This confuses the word with comprise, which describes the parts that make up a whole.

practice.prompt: A band's two singers each want to perform a different song at the school concert.
options: Eight songs compromise the concert's full program this year.
The two singers compromise beautifully, so their voices blend in perfect harmony.
The singers agreed to compromise by performing a shortened version of both songs.
To compromise, each singer insisted on singing only her own song.
reasons: This mistakes the word for comprise; listing a program's parts involves no disagreement.
Singing in harmony is a musical skill, not a settlement in which each side gives something up.
Each singer accepts less than her full wish, so both make a concession to settle the dispute.
Two people holding firm without yielding have not settled anything.
